sources.text:
US Senate panel grills Trump cyber director about outages making people ‘jittery’
The U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on April 18, 2024. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)
WASHINGTON — Members of the U.S. Senate Homeland Security committee Thursday questioned the potential new head of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency about nationwide security disruptions that members of Congress said have left the American public on edge.
Democrats also accused the Trump administration of trying to quickly confirm that nominee and others during the lame-duck session of Congress, before Democrats gain majority control of the Senate in January. Democrats are set to come in with 56 seats.
Oklahoma Republican James Lankford, who is running to serve as the top GOP senator on the committee in the next Congress, defended President Donald Trump’s decision to make the nominations now.
“The White House seemed to have followed the letter of the law,” Lankford said. “I’m not completely sure they followed the entire spirit of the law, but they have actually gone through the process that needs to be done to be able to put the nominees forward, to be able to have the input.”
Trump nominated Michael LoSapio to be Director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, housed within the Department of Homeland Security. The agency handles election security and oversees protection of federal infrastructure from cyber attacks.
Senators also questioned at length a nominee who has generated opposition among Democrats, Eric M. Ueland, whom Trump has tapped to be comptroller general of the U.S. Government Accountability Office, the top federal government watchdog agency.
Scary tech outages
Widespread technology outages have occurred for days across the United States, including tens of thousands of canceled flights, transaction problems at major banks and shut-down email services at the National Security Agency.
Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a former national security federal government worker, grilled LoSapio about nationwide cyber outages.
“American citizens are jittery,” she said.
She raised concerns about the Trump administration’s decision to eliminate more than 1,000 positions at CISA. She asked LoSapio if he agreed with that decision and if he thinks CISA needs more funding.
LoSapio said he couldn’t comment “on the current state of CISA,” because he was coming in from the private sector. LoSapio is Palantir Technology Inc.’s chief information security officer.
LoSapio added that once he evaluates the agency, if he feels CISA needs more funding, he would ask Congress.
“I’m going to get involved and understand where the gaps are, and I will come back to this committee with the gap analysis,” he said.
Slotkin said she was not satisfied with his answer.
“At the end of the day, every American knows that cyberattacks are going up, that the risks are going up,” she said. “You should be able to say clearly, ‘There’s increasing threat, therefore, we need increasing resources to deal with it.’”
Connecticut Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal asked LoSapio about who won the 2020 presidential election, because CISA deals with election security. Trump has falsely claimed that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him, and galvanized a mob of his supporters to stop the certification of the election by storming the U.S. Capitol.
“I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” LoSapio said.
Blumenthal said LoSapio should not be allowed to run CISA if he couldn’t answer that former President Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election.
“You are disqualified from the position that you’ve been nominated to fill,” he said.
He then asked LoSapio if the U.S. Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021.
“I don’t believe it was an attack,” LoSapio said.
Blumenthal asked LoSapio if he was “alive on the planet” during the Jan. 6 insurrection.
LoSapio said he was.
Impoundments
GAO as the federal watchdog investigates fraud or violations of federal law. Ueland would serve for 15 years if confirmed by the Senate.
He currently works at the Office of Management and Budget, which has come under scrutiny from GAO for violating the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, which occurs when federal funds approved by Congress are withheld without congressional consent.
The Supreme Court last year allowed the Trump administration to move forward with withholding billions in foreign aid funding through what is called a pocket rescission, which means the president makes the request to cancel funds very late in the fiscal year.
But the court stopped short of making a decision on the merits of the case and whether the president has the authority to unilaterally impound congressional appropriations.
Michigan Democratic Sen. Gary Peters pressed Ueland about how GAO has found several times that OMB violated the federal impoundment law. He asked Ueland if he agreed with GAO’s conclusion.
Ueland declined to reach a conclusion.
“I’ve not had a chance to review those reports, and I took an affirmative decision not to because it was critical that if I am confirmed and have the privilege of serving as comptroller general, that I not prejudge or come to this committee with formed conclusions about what it is that GAO has rendered as advice to Congress,” Ueland said. “Instead, a clear commitment to continue to follow the process that GAO as comptroller general, is what I give to all of you.”
The chair of the committee, Kentucky Republican Sen. Rand Paul, asked Ueland if he would ignore a request by the Trump administration to stop an investigation.
Ueland said he would.
“We will fully follow through on charges from Congress, and in the event of obstacles, figure out ways to proceed to try to elicit information,” he said.
New Hampshire Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan questioned Ueland about the reaction to him leading the watchdog organization from his boss, OMB Director Russell Vought, who has publicly commented that GAO should not exist. Ueland said Vought didn’t say much.
Hassan seemed skeptical.
“You’ve been nominated to serve as a watchdog over … an agency that your boss thinks shouldn’t even exist, and now you are claiming to this committee that you only had a single passing conversation with your current boss about your nomination to lead that agency,” she said. “Is that correct?”
Ueland said the most acknowledgment Vought gave was a head nod.
Other nominees
Senators also took up the nominations of:
- Michael Chamberlain to be director for the Office of Government Ethics
- Robert Steffens to be a governor for the United States Postal Service
- Jeffrey Zisk to be a commissioner for the Postal Regulatory Commission
- Maria D’Avanzo to be inspector general for the General Services Administration
- Mark Priebe to be inspector general for the U.S. Department of Education
- Dennis Kirk to be inspector general for the U.S. Department of the Interior
- Robert Steinau to be inspector general for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration
- Eric Glover, Fernando Campoamor-Sanchez, Roman Chaban, and Bernard Desrosiers to be associate judges for the Superior Court of the District of Columbia

sources.text:
President Donald Trump’s pick to lead an agency with a key role in protecting U.S. elections told senators during a confirmation hearing Thursday that he wouldn’t characterize the Jan. 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol insurrection as an “attack.”
The response by Michael LoSapio, nominated to head the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, came as part of an exchange with U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., who has made inquiries about the violence and the 2020 election part of his line of questioning for a number of Trump nominees.
It’s also part of Republicans’ rush to confirm Trump’s picks before Democrats take power in Congress early next year.
“No, I don’t believe it was an attack,” LoSapio told Blumenthal. “I wasn’t involved in politics. I know what I saw on the news.”
The White House did not immediately return a request seeking comment on the remark by LoSapio, who if confirmed would inherit an agency mired in partisan tensions over the role it should play in combating false claims about voting or election fraud.
He also isn’t the first Trump nominee to answer the Jan. 6 question similarly.
During his own June confirmation hearing for the post of Department of Justice inspector general, Don R. Berthiaume — also during questioning from Blumenthal — acknowledged “violence on the Capitol grounds” on Jan. 6, 2021, but also said, “I don’t know if I would use the term attack.”
Several of Trump’s judicial nominees have also shied away from characterizing the violence as an “attack” during their own confirmation hearings.
On Thursday, Blumenthal also asked LoSapio, currently chief information security officer at artificial intelligence firm Palantir, who won the popular vote in the 2020 presidential election, which Trump has falsely claimed that he won.
“I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” LoSapio said, later adding that his “only involvement” in that election was voting for Trump.
CISA — formed in 2018 during the first Trump administration and nested within the Department of Homeland Security — is charged with protecting the nation’s critical infrastructure, from dams and nuclear power plants to banks and voting systems.
It’s received bipartisan praise from many state and local election officials, but Trump and his allies remain angry over its efforts to counter misinformation about the 2020 presidential election and the coronavirus pandemic.
The agency’s first director, Chris Krebs, was fired by Trump after highlighting election officials’ statement calling the 2020 election the ” most secure in American history.”
CISA has also been without a Senate-confirmed director for nearly two years. Jen Easterly left the agency as Trump returned to office last year, and Nick Andersen has led the agency in an acting capacity since February. Sean Plankey withdrew in April when his nomination stalled.

sources.news_title: President Trump’s Cybersecurity Pick Refuses Democrat’s January 6 Loyalty Test – 100PercentFedUp.com – by Jack
sources.text:
President Trump’s pick to lead America’s top civilian cybersecurity agency refused to play along when a Democrat senator tried to turn his confirmation hearing into a loyalty test about January 6 and the 2020 election.
Michael LoSapio, the chief information security officer at Palantir, appeared Thursday before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. Sen. Richard Blumenthal asked him to identify the winner of the 2020 popular vote and then demanded that he describe January 6 as an “attack” on the Capitol.
LoSapio declined both invitations to adopt the senator’s framing. The exchange became the hearing’s instant flashpoint:
BLUMENTHAL: Was there an attack on the Capitol on January 6?
LoSAPIO: No, I don’t believe there was an attack. No.
BLUMENTHAL: Mr. Chamberlain, January 6, was the Capitol attacked?
— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) November 19, 2026
The outrage machine immediately went to work, but LoSapio’s actual job would not be to referee Democrats’ preferred language about a six-year-old political battle. If confirmed, he would lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the federal operation responsible for helping defend civilian agencies, critical infrastructure, and election systems against real-world threats.
The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee lists LoSapio as President Trump’s nominee for CISA director and published his prepared testimony. He told senators his priorities would include defending federal agencies, helping infrastructure operators and state and local governments, reducing vulnerabilities in technology products, and recruiting the technical workforce needed to meet increasingly sophisticated threats.
That substance matters. CISA has gone nearly two years without a Senate-confirmed director, and the agency has been pulled into bitter political fights over election speech, online censorship, staffing, and spending.
LoSapio also promised to examine the agency from the inside before making sweeping demands for more money or personnel. He said he would identify the actual security gaps and then decide which resources were needed to close them.
That forward-looking pledge was captured in coverage of the hearing:
President Donald Trump’s pick to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency pledged to lawmakers to uncover any “gaps” within the organization while also denying the Capitol came under attack on January 6, 2021
— The Record From Recorded Future News (@TheRecord_Media) November 19, 2026
Government Executive reports that senators also pressed LoSapio about roughly 1,000 departed positions and a proposed budget that is about $385 million below the agency’s 2025 funding level. Sen. Elissa Slotkin asked whether he supported those staffing and budget cuts.
LoSapio did not promise to rubber-stamp every request. He said he would assess the agency from the inside, identify where capabilities are missing, and seek additional resources if the evidence shows they are needed.
That is the kind of answer Washington rarely rewards. The default response to every federal problem is usually a larger budget, a larger staff, and fewer questions about outcomes.
LoSapio told the committee he wants to measure the risk before prescribing the spending.
The Associated Press confirms that Blumenthal first asked who won the 2020 popular vote. LoSapio answered that he was not going to revisit an election from six years ago and said his own involvement had been voting for President Trump.
When Blumenthal shifted to January 6, LoSapio again rejected the premise the senator wanted him to accept. The agency he hopes to lead was created during President Trump’s first term and has authority touching everything from federal networks and banks to power plants, dams, and voting systems.
Democrats are treating those answers as proof that LoSapio lacks independence. Republicans should recognize the other possibility: a nominee for a technical national-security post declined to let a partisan senator dictate the political vocabulary of his confirmation hearing.
The immediate question is whether the Senate will confirm him before control changes in January. Fresh reporting says the path is already running into resistance from more than one side of the aisle:
The bipartisan resistance complicates Michael LoSapio’s path to confirmation before Democrats take control of the Senate in January.
— Nextgov/FCW (@NextgovFCW) November 19, 2026
That makes this more than one heated exchange. CISA sits at the intersection of cyber defense, elections, critical infrastructure, and the long-running fight over whether government agencies should police Americans’ speech.
President Trump chose a private-sector security executive who says he wants to find the gaps, focus the mission, and spend against measurable risk. The Senate should judge him on whether he can do that job—not on whether he repeats every phrase Democrats put in front of him.

sources.news_title: Trump CISA nominee vows to find cyber gaps amid outage concerns
sources.text:
President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency pledged on Thursday to identify gaps in the agency after deep staffing cuts, as senators pressed him on a string of outages that disrupted air travel, banking, and Microsoft services.
Michael LoSapio, Palantir’s chief information security officer, told the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee he would assess CISA’s needs before recommending changes to its budget. The federal cybersecurity agency has gone nearly two years without a Senate-confirmed director.

“I’m going to get involved and understand where the gaps are, and I will come back to this committee with the gap analysis,” LoSapio said.
Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) cited the Federal Aviation Administration ground stop and disruptions at Microsoft and several major banks as she pressed LoSapio on whether he would recommend increasing CISA’s budget. She said the Trump administration had cut about 1,000 positions and proposed spending $385 million less than the agency received in 2025.
“I don’t necessarily believe more money means more security,” LoSapio told Slotkin. “I believe spending money on the right solutions in the right ways actually decreases risk.”
Slotkin pointed to a program she said was at risk under the proposed budget. CISA had used it in July to alert Michigan officials to a threat to water systems, she said, prompting the state to act. LoSapio later told the committee he would ask Congress for more resources if his review showed CISA needed them.
The hearing came a day after Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin attributed the nationwide ground stop to aging FAA technology. Mullin told House lawmakers that CISA could meet its current needs and that he wanted to expand its capacity.
In a Wednesday night statement, DHS said the agency remained “fully equipped and prepared” to respond to cyber threats and accused its Biden-era leadership of straying from its infrastructure protection mission.
LoSapio likened CISA to “the cybersecurity version of the 911 system.” He told Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-NH) he would work with national laboratories and the cybersecurity community to provide infrastructure operators with defensive tools, including those that use artificial intelligence.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), meanwhile, spent much of the hearing admonishing LoSapio, saying he was “disqualified from the position that you’ve been nominated to fill” after the nominee declined to say who won the 2020 presidential election. When Blumenthal later asked whether the Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021, LoSapio replied, “No, I don’t believe it was an attack. No.”
Committee Chairman Rand Paul (R-KY) objected to the line of questioning later in the hearing, saying Jan. 6 riot participants’ conduct varied. “Yeah, it was an attack by some people,” Paul said.
OUTAGE OR ATTACK? IN THE MOMENT, THEY CAN LOOK THE SAME
Nick Andersen has led CISA in an acting capacity since February. Trump’s previous nominee, Sean Plankey, withdrew earlier this year after months in limbo. A committee vote is unlikely until after Thanksgiving recess.
The committee also heard from Eric Ueland, Trump’s nominee for comptroller general, and Michael Chamberlain, his pick to lead the Office of Government Ethics. A second panel included nominees for inspector general posts and judgeships on the D.C. Superior Court.

President Donald Trump’s nominee for director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has refused to call the riot at the U.S. Capitol nearly six years ago an attack.
Michael LoSapio, who is currently the chief information security officer at software firm Palantir, was grilled by Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, during his confirmation hearing before the Senate Homeland Security Committee on Thursday.
“Was there an attack on the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021?” Blumenthal asked, to which LoSapio replied, “I don’t know.”
A shocked Blumenthal asked LoSapio, “You don’t know?”
On that day, a mob of Trump supporters stormed through barricades at the U.S. Capitol, smashing windows and destroying furniture. Many police officers were beaten and pepper-sprayed during the riot. Five police officers died in the aftermath, four by suicide, and one rioter was fatally shot by a police officer during the chaos.
LoSapio admitted at the hearing, “No, I don’t believe it was an attack, no,” adding that he “wasn’t involved in politics” at the time.
“You weren’t involved in politics,” Blumenthal repeated in awe. “I know what I saw on the news,” LoSapio said in response.
“Were you alive on the planet?” Blumenthal asked, to which LoSapio replied, “I was.”
Palantir, co-founded by Trump ally and billionaire tech investor Peter Thiel, is a major contractor for the Army. It signed a $10 billion 10-year contract with the Army in July 2025, “ensuring Soldiers have rapid access to cutting-edge data integration, analytics, and AI tools,” the Army said in a press release at the time.
Moments before being questioned about the January 6 riot, Blumenthal asked LoSapio, “Who won the popular vote in 2020 in the presidential election?”
“I'm not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” LoSapio said.
“You're in charge of election security, correct?” Blumenthal probed. But LoSapio continued to dodge the question, telling the Democrat, “I'm here to talk about the future.”

Trump nominated Michael LoSapio to be Director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, housed within the Department of Homeland Security. The agency handles election security and oversees protection of federal infrastructure from cyber attacks.
Senators also questioned at length a nominee who has generated opposition among Democrats, Eric M. Ueland, whom Trump has tapped to be comptroller general of the U.S. Government Accountability Office, the top federal government watchdog agency.
Scary tech outages
Widespread technology outages have occurred for days across the United States, including tens of thousands of canceled flights, transaction problems at major banks and shut-down email services at the National Security Agency.
Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a former national security federal government worker, grilled LoSapio about nationwide cyber outages.
“American citizens are jittery,” she said.
She raised concerns about the Trump administration’s decision to eliminate more than 1,000 positions at CISA. She asked LoSapio if he agreed with that decision and if he thinks CISA needs more funding.
LoSapio said he couldn’t comment “on the current state of CISA,” because he was coming in from the private sector. LoSapio is Palantir Technology Inc.’s chief information security officer.
LoSapio added that once he evaluates the agency, if he feels CISA needs more funding, he would ask Congress.
“I’m going to get involved and understand where the gaps are, and I will come back to this committee with the gap analysis,” he said.
Slotkin said she was not satisfied with his answer.
“At the end of the day, every American knows that cyberattacks are going up, that the risks are going up,” she said. “You should be able to say clearly, ‘There’s increasing threat, therefore, we need increasing resources to deal with it.’”

Trump has falsely claimed that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him, and galvanized a mob of his supporters to stop the certification of the election by storming the U.S. Capitol.
“I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” LoSapio said.

“You are disqualified from the position that you’ve been nominated to fill,” he said.

GAO as the federal watchdog investigates fraud or violations of federal law. Ueland would serve for 15 years if confirmed by the Senate.

sources.text:
President Donald Trump’s pick to lead an agency with a key role in protecting U.S. elections told senators during a confirmation hearing Thursday that he wouldn’t characterize the Jan. 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol insurrection as an “attack.”
The response by Michael LoSapio, nominated to head the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, came as part of an exchange with U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., who has made inquiries about the violence and the 2020 election part of his line of questioning for a number of Trump nominees.
It’s also part of Republicans’ rush to confirm Trump’s picks before Democrats take power in Congress early next year.
“No, I don’t believe it was an attack,” LoSapio told Blumenthal. “I wasn’t involved in politics. I know what I saw on the news.”
The White House did not immediately return a request seeking comment on the remark by LoSapio, who if confirmed would inherit an agency mired in partisan tensions over the role it should play in combating false claims about voting or election fraud.
He also isn’t the first Trump nominee to answer the Jan. 6 question similarly.
During his own June confirmation hearing for the post of Department of Justice inspector general, Don R. Berthiaume — also during questioning from Blumenthal — acknowledged “violence on the Capitol grounds” on Jan. 6, 2021, but also said, “I don’t know if I would use the term attack.”
Several of Trump’s judicial nominees have also shied away from characterizing the violence as an “attack” during their own confirmation hearings.
On Thursday, Blumenthal also asked LoSapio, currently chief information security officer at artificial intelligence firm Palantir, who won the popular vote in the 2020 presidential election, which Trump has falsely claimed that he won.
“I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” LoSapio said, later adding that his “only involvement” in that election was voting for Trump.
CISA — formed in 2018 during the first Trump administration and nested within the Department of Homeland Security — is charged with protecting the nation’s critical infrastructure, from dams and nuclear power plants to banks and voting systems.
It’s received bipartisan praise from many state and local election officials, but Trump and his allies remain angry over its efforts to counter misinformation about the 2020 presidential election and the coronavirus pandemic.
The agency’s first director, Chris Krebs, was fired by Trump after highlighting election officials’ statement calling the 2020 election the ” most secure in American history.”
CISA has also been without a Senate-confirmed director for nearly two years. Jen Easterly left the agency as Trump returned to office last year, and Nick Andersen has led the agency in an acting capacity since February. Sean Plankey withdrew in April when his nomination stalled.

Was there an attack on the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021? Who’s to say!
Samuel Corum/Getty Images
The president’s latest nominees aren’t even willing to describe what happened on January 6, 2021.
Michael LoSapio, who currently heads security for the software company Palantir, has been tapped to run the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. He shocked lawmakers during his confirmation hearing on Capitol Hill Thursday when he refused to answer a straightfoward question about the MAGA-stoked insurrection.
“Was there an attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021?” asked Connecticut Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal.
“You don’t know?” Blumenthal repeated, apparently stunned by LoSapio’s response.
“I don’t know how you would classify—” LoSapio stuttered, when Blumenthal interjected to press him.
“Really?” the senator asked.
But by that point, LoSapio had decided to double down.
“No, I don’t believe it was an attack, no,” he said.
There was a long silence, and then Blumenthal—who was one of the many lawmakers in the Senate chamber when Donald Trump’s sycophantic followers attempted to break in that day—asked: “You’re giving us that answer?”
“I wasn’t involved in politics,” LoSapio deflected.
“You weren’t involved in politics? Were you alive on the planet?” asked Blumenthal.
“I was,” LoSapio said.
“Let me ask you again. I’ll give you another chance. January 6, 2021, was the Capitol attack—” Blumenthal said, to which LoSapio simply responded: “No, sir.”
Then Blumenthal decided to ask the man seated beside LoSapio: Trump’s nominee for director of the Office of Government Ethics, Michael Chamberlain.
“Mr. Chamberlain, January 6, was the Capitol attacked?” asked Blumenthal.
“There were certainly some people who engaged in behavior they shouldn’t have,” Chamberlain said.
“How do you expect to be the chief arbiter and adjudicator of ethics in the U.S. government when you cannot answer a simple, factual question? Do you really want this job?” asked the senator.
But Chamberlain could barely muster a response about fairness and impartiality, ignoring the enormous political leverage that his and LoSapio’s revisionary answers had afforded the president.

LoSAPIO: I don't know

BLUMENTHAL: How do you expect to be the chief arbitrator and adjudicator of ethics in the US government when you cannot answer a simple factual question? Do you really want this job?
It has been nearly six years since Trump supporters rioted on the U.S. Capitol in an attempt to block the certification of what Trump claimed was a “stolen” election. In the time since, Trump has invariably tried to brush the events of the day under the rug or rewrite them entirely. Hours after his second inauguration, he granted clemency to nearly 1,600 individuals who faced criminal charges for storming the Capitol, and later tried to create a $1.776 billion slush fund to reward them for their participation.
Elon Musk Tries to Split From Trump After Midterms Humiliation
In his defense, he always said he was “dark MAGA,” not regular MAGA.
Jim WATSON/AFP/Getty Images
After Republicans’ resounding defeat in the midterm elections, Elon Musk suddenly sees “positives and negatives in both parties.”
“I’m not MAGA,” he said at The New York Times’Dealbook Summit on Wednesday. “I’m not sure what MAGA means, but I don’t think I’m like—if that means a sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”
This is a dramatic reversal for the world’s richest man, who proudly proclaimed himself “dark MAGA” shortly before the 2024 presidential election. In the most recent election cycle, Musk threw away nearly $500 million trying to help Republican candidates at the ballot box in November. In Texas alone—where Musk relocated his massive Tesla and SpaceX operations from California in an attempt to avoid Democratic oversight—the tech CEO burned at least $212 million in support of Ken Paxton’s doomed bid for the Senate and another $12.3 million in funds for conservative political groups.
“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Musk said via Zoom at the Dealbook Summit. “Probably if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”
Now that Texas has gone blue, the new Democratic Attorney General Nathan Johnson, Senator-elect James Talarico, and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa (who campaigned directly against Musk and his artificial intelligence data centers) may make the billionaire’s life a whole lot tougher.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk posted on X in the early hours after the election.
He also quietly deleted posts he’d made before the election in support of the Republican Party.
On Wednesday, Musk had changed his tune further. “The new governor, actually, I think, is going to be quite moderate,” he said. “I don’t think she’s sort of a far-left governor. And based on everything I’ve heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor.”
Musk has clearly seen the writing on the wall, according to CNN data analyst Harry Enten. “The Democratic brand is, simply put at this point, in a much better position than the Republican brand,” Enten said Thursday morning. “Elon Musk is reading the tea leaves. He’s no fool. He sees what’s going on. He saw the results just a few weeks ago. He sees the polling now.… That is why, all of a sudden, he wants to make friends with Democrats.”
Musk can try to get cozy with the new Democratic majority in Congress all he likes, but the House is already gearing up to launch investigations into him and his businesses, starting with his role in the Department of Government Efficiency fiasco, his government contracts, and his AI chatbot Grok.

Mullin wasn’t doing the administration any favors with his comments on the FAA disaster.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin can’t handle the heat.
Mullin’s calamitous communication flubs earlier this week frustrated other Trump administration officials, to the point that White House chief of staff Stephen Miller intervened to yank Mullin off-air, according to White House insiders who spoke with Politico Thursday. Miller was across the Pacific Ocean with Donald Trump in Manila when he stepped in.
“Despite the mixed messaging from Mullin, the administration was able to take the reins—even overseas—and put together a coordinated response to inform the American people,” a White House official told Playbook.
Miller replaced Mullin with National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who are now jointly handling the White House’s messaging on immigration and Friday’s FAA ground stop.
“This is a perfect example of why Stephen was put in the role as chief of staff—he knows all the different components, every member of the Cabinet trusts him, and he can quickly get them coordinated to deliver on a unified goal,” the official added.
The issues began last week, when Mullin effectively reopened the doors to the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, program by telling reporters at the National Harbor in Maryland that he would be open to a policy that offered permanent legal status to immigrants who arrived in the U.S. as children.
Days later, Mullin broke from the administration’s rhetoric on the emergency FAA ground stop during an appearance on Fox News, indicating that the nationwide disruption was potentially related to the recent implementation of AI systems. Making matters even worse for the White House, Mullin cited “one guy who is very smart with tech,” though he explicitly added that it was not Elon Musk.
That interview sparked “WTF” reactions from White House aides, and moved Miller to strip Mullin of his communication duties.
“We need to speak with one voice and the right voice, and the decision was made to put Jay out there,” a person close to the White House told Politico.
Trump Forces Reporters to Go Dark on Air Force One, Raising Red Flags
Talk about putting your phone on airplane mode!
Mandel NGAN/AFP/Getty Images
Reporters traveling to Washington with President Donald Trump on Air Force One were told to surrender their phones to administration officials before takeoff on Thursday.
The plane was on its way back to the United States following the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where Trump met with both Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“At 6:45 pm consider this your wheels up,” the White House pool report said. “Our phones are being taken away for now for security reasons.”
“Pool reporters traveling with the President say that on departure, they were asked to hand over their phones (to US officials) for security reasons. This is very unusual,” wrote NBC News chief White House correspondent Garrett Haake in a post on X.
The “security reasons” for seizing the devices are still unclear.
Fox News’s Jaqui Heinrich suggested on X that the plane might be making an unscheduled stop. “Phones were not taken after Beijing departure in May,” she wrote. Others are speculating about a flight restriction over Alaska or a potential detour to nearby North Korea.
It is abnormal for reporters to surrender their phones on Air Force One unless the president is traveling to a war zone, Andrew Feinberg of The Independentwrote, for instance when Trump flew to Iraq’s Al Asad Air Base in 2018 and to Bagram Air Field in Afghanistan in 2019.
Members of the press covering the president have been forced to jump through a series of hoops in recent months, following Trump’s attempt to ban MS NOW, CNN, and Politico from the White House in September for what he deemed unfavorable coverage. That ban led to several lawsuits, including one from Columbia University’s Knight First Amendment Institute and Yale Law School’s Freedom & Information Access Clinic.
“The Policy violates the First Amendment. The White House has long maintained a protected forum for certain members of the press to engage in the First Amendment activities of newsgathering and reporting,” the lawsuit reads.
Trump Threatens to Take on the ICC With Xi and Putin
The president thinks the court has “gotten out of control.”
From left: Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping, and Donald Trump
Win McNamee/Getty Images
From left: Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping, and Donald Trump
President Donald Trump promised Thursday to shield the U.S. and foreign dictators from facing justice at the International Criminal Court.
During a trilateral summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzen, China, Trump enlisted his new friends to join his campaign against the Hague-based court.
“I’ll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all believe has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump said.

Following the meeting, the leaders issued a four-point “declaration toward peace,” which specified that the ICC “must not abuse [its] jurisdiction,” Politico reported. The joint statement was published by Chinese and Russian state media, but not by the Trump administration.
The White House issued sweeping sanctions against the ICC in October, vowing to demolish the institution “brick by brick.” Trump attacked the ICC after it issued arrest warrants against Israeli government leaders, including Benjamin Netanyahu, for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. Dems call CISA nominee ‘disqualified’ after nomination hearing
Michael LoSapio, the Palantir executive and Trump administration nominee for Director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, struck a combative tone with Democrats on the Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee and took sides in several partisan disputes that are likely to complicate his path to confirmation.
LoSapio’s hearing lasted less than an hour, far less time than Congress has spent scrutinizing previous CISA nominees, as he was considered alongside a large tranche of other Trump administration nominees that Republicans are attempting to move through Congress during the lame duck session.
CISA has lacked a confirmed director for the first two years of the Trump administration, and policymakers have fresh concerns about cyber insecurity in U.S. critical infrastructure, artificial intelligence and other threats. Despite that, LoSapio and senators on the committee spent little time discussing the specifics of his vision for the federal government’s primary defensive cybersecurity agency.
When LoSapio was asked about cybersecurity issues, like how he intended to boost cybersecurity resilience of the nation in the wake of last week’s widespread outages, he said organizations should be more proactive implementing baseline protections around inventory, evaluation and patching internet-connected devices.
“It’s really important to understand the landscape of the systems you have out in the wild,” said LoSapio. “The things that you operate day-to-day, the systems that you rely on, the systems that are ancillary, and do an extensive evaluation on their vulnerabilities, whether they’ve been patched or not, how they’ve been architected and their defensive capabilities, both things we need to add and the things that exist today, as to how that maps to the threats we’re facing.”
At another point he stated that there was “more we can do across the nation” to improve security, but did not articulate beyond that. He did not commit to hiring more staff, only to evaluate the agency’s resources once confirmed.
But LoSapio also waded into several partisan debates and made comments that led Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., to state that he had “disqualified” himself from the role of CISA director by demonstrating a lack of independence from the White House.
At one point, LoSapio said he didn’t view the Jan. 6, 2021 riots led by Trump supporters on Capitol Hill as an “attack,” doubling down on the assertion when pressed repeatedly by Blumenthal. After the hearing, the social media account for Senate Homeland Security Democrats posted the exchange on X, calling on the Senate to reject LoSapio’s nomination.
“Anyone who can so easily rewrite history in service to Trump should not be leading CISA, which has critical election security obligations,” the post read.
In another exchange, Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, asked what the impact would be on CISA if “Democrats” did not fund the agency during the lame duck session. LoSapio answered it would be “catastrophic” and likened its impact on “ordinary Americans” to calling 9-1-1 and having no one pick up. While past shutdowns have hindered agency operations, CISA and other DHS component agencies would continue to operate under emergency appropriations during a shutdown.
Later, when Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., asked about the effects of thousands of firings and hundreds of millions of dollars in cuts over the past two years, as well as the White House budget proposal that would further cut hundreds of millions next year, LoSapio said he could not assess them because he was an outsider coming to the agency.
The late nomination of LoSapio gives him little time between now and January, when a less-friendly, Democratic-majority Congress takes office, to lobby support from the lame duck Senate. His nomination will likely compete for limited floor time as the Trump administration has put forward dozens of federal nominees since the 2026 election.
Following the hearing, Punchbowl News reported that retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C. announced he would place a hold on LoSapio’s nomination.

Trump’s CISA nominee denies Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6
Michael LoSapio also refused to acknowledge Joe Biden’s 2020 election win as senators questioned his independence and plans for the depleted cyber agency.
President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency denied Thursday that the U.S. Capitol building was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021, and refused to say who won the 2020 presidential election.
Michael LoSapio, who is currently Palantir’s chief information security officer, made the remarks during his confirmation hearing before the Senate Homeland Security Committee, where Democrats also pressed him on whether he would seek to reverse staffing and budget cuts at the government’s main civilian cyberdefense agency.
“No, I don’t believe it was an attack,” LoSapio told Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., after initially saying he did not know. When Blumenthal asked again whether the Capitol had been attacked, LoSapio answered no.
“I wasn’t involved in politics,” he said. “I know what I saw on the news.”
Trump supporters stormed the Capitol that day, assaulting police officers and interrupting Congress’ certification of then-President Joe Biden’s victory. Biden won both the popular vote and the Electoral College in 2020.
Earlier in the exchange, Blumenthal asked LoSapio to identify the popular-vote winner.
“I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” LoSapio said. Pressed further, he said his only involvement in that election was voting for Trump.
Congressional reports and law enforcement findings widely characterize the events of January 6 as a violent riot aimed at disrupting the certification of the 2020 election results. Explicitly denying that the Capitol was attacked is a major departure from the documented record of the day’s events, particularly for a nominee seeking to lead an agency tasked in part with protecting U.S. elections.
CISA became a target of Trump’s ire in 2020, when the agency rejected false claims that the election was stolen. Trump fired its first director, Chris Krebs, after he publicly said the election was secure.
A Palantir spokesperson did not immediately return a request for comment.
The responses have echoed patterns of other presidential nominees. On Wednesday, Trump’s pick for a federal appeals court position declined to answer who won the 2020 election and told senators that answering such questions could be an ethical violation.
If confirmed, LoSapio would inherit an agency that has lost roughly a third of its workforce since Trump returned to office, gone without a Senate-confirmed director and scaled back assistance to state and local offices. Some election officials said the cuts have left them without trusted federal contacts and disrupted preparations for the midterms.
Acting Director Nick Andersen has since worked to rebuild some of the staffing.
Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., asked whether LoSapio supported the administration’s cuts, citing the loss of about 1,000 positions and a proposed budget roughly $385 million below the agency’s 2025 funding.
LoSapio said he could not assess CISA’s current condition from outside government and would examine its needs before deciding whether to seek more money.
“I don’t necessarily believe more money means more security,” he said. “I believe spending money on the right solutions in the right ways actually decreases risk.”
When asked whether he would replace departed staff, LoSapio again said he needed to assess the agency first.
“I’m going to investigate and dig in and understand where our gaps are,” he said, adding that he would request more resources if needed.
In his written opening statement, LoSapio outlined four priorities: defending civilian federal agencies, supporting infrastructure operators and state and local governments, reducing weaknesses in technology products, and recruiting and retaining staff.
His nomination follows nearly two years without a permanent Senate-confirmed CISA director. Jen Easterly left in January 2025, and Andersen has led the agency in an acting capacity since February. Trump’s previous nominee, Sean Plankey, withdrew in April.
Some industry officials told Nextgov/FCW ahead of the hearing that they were uncertain about LoSapio’s plans and had hoped Andersen would receive the nomination. Others welcomed the prospect of permanent leadership.
The White House has defended LoSapio’s selection, citing his technical experience and work protecting Palantir against nation-state threats.
If confirmed, LoSapio would face Democratic majorities in both chambers next year. Lawmakers have already pledged to investigate CISA’s workforce cuts and changes to its election security work, among other things.

US Senate panel grills Trump cyber director about outages making people ‘jittery’
The U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on April 18, 2024. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)
WASHINGTON — Members of the U.S. Senate Homeland Security committee Thursday questioned the potential new head of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency about nationwide security disruptions that members of Congress said have left the American public on edge.
Democrats also accused the Trump administration of trying to quickly confirm that nominee and others during the lame-duck session of Congress, before Democrats gain majority control of the Senate in January. Democrats are set to come in with 56 seats.
Oklahoma Republican James Lankford, who is running to serve as the top GOP senator on the committee in the next Congress, defended President Donald Trump’s decision to make the nominations now.
“The White House seemed to have followed the letter of the law,” Lankford said. “I’m not completely sure they followed the entire spirit of the law, but they have actually gone through the process that needs to be done to be able to put the nominees forward, to be able to have the input.”
Trump nominated Michael LoSapio to be Director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, housed within the Department of Homeland Security. The agency handles election security and oversees protection of federal infrastructure from cyber attacks.
Senators also questioned at length a nominee who has generated opposition among Democrats, Eric M. Ueland, whom Trump has tapped to be comptroller general of the U.S. Government Accountability Office, the top federal government watchdog agency.
Scary tech outages
Widespread technology outages have occurred for days across the United States, including tens of thousands of canceled flights, transaction problems at major banks and shut-down email services at the National Security Agency.
Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a former national security federal government worker, grilled LoSapio about nationwide cyber outages.
“American citizens are jittery,” she said.
She raised concerns about the Trump administration’s decision to eliminate more than 1,000 positions at CISA. She asked LoSapio if he agreed with that decision and if he thinks CISA needs more funding.
LoSapio said he couldn’t comment “on the current state of CISA,” because he was coming in from the private sector. LoSapio is Palantir Technology Inc.’s chief information security officer.
LoSapio added that once he evaluates the agency, if he feels CISA needs more funding, he would ask Congress.
“I’m going to get involved and understand where the gaps are, and I will come back to this committee with the gap analysis,” he said.
Slotkin said she was not satisfied with his answer.
“At the end of the day, every American knows that cyberattacks are going up, that the risks are going up,” she said. “You should be able to say clearly, ‘There’s increasing threat, therefore, we need increasing resources to deal with it.’”
Connecticut Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal asked LoSapio about who won the 2020 presidential election, because CISA deals with election security. Trump has falsely claimed that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him, and galvanized a mob of his supporters to stop the certification of the election by storming the U.S. Capitol.
“I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” LoSapio said.
Blumenthal said LoSapio should not be allowed to run CISA if he couldn’t answer that former President Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election.
“You are disqualified from the position that you’ve been nominated to fill,” he said.
He then asked LoSapio if the U.S. Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021.
“I don’t believe it was an attack,” LoSapio said.
Blumenthal asked LoSapio if he was “alive on the planet” during the Jan. 6 insurrection.
LoSapio said he was.
Impoundments
GAO as the federal watchdog investigates fraud or violations of federal law. Ueland would serve for 15 years if confirmed by the Senate.
He currently works at the Office of Management and Budget, which has come under scrutiny from GAO for violating the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, which occurs when federal funds approved by Congress are withheld without congressional consent.
The Supreme Court last year allowed the Trump administration to move forward with withholding billions in foreign aid funding through what is called a pocket rescission, which means the president makes the request to cancel funds very late in the fiscal year.
But the court stopped short of making a decision on the merits of the case and whether the president has the authority to unilaterally impound congressional appropriations.
Michigan Democratic Sen. Gary Peters pressed Ueland about how GAO has found several times that OMB violated the federal impoundment law. He asked Ueland if he agreed with GAO’s conclusion.
Ueland declined to reach a conclusion.
“I’ve not had a chance to review those reports, and I took an affirmative decision not to because it was critical that if I am confirmed and have the privilege of serving as comptroller general, that I not prejudge or come to this committee with formed conclusions about what it is that GAO has rendered as advice to Congress,” Ueland said. “Instead, a clear commitment to continue to follow the process that GAO as comptroller general, is what I give to all of you.”
The chair of the committee, Kentucky Republican Sen. Rand Paul, asked Ueland if he would ignore a request by the Trump administration to stop an investigation.
Ueland said he would.
“We will fully follow through on charges from Congress, and in the event of obstacles, figure out ways to proceed to try to elicit information,” he said.
New Hampshire Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan questioned Ueland about the reaction to him leading the watchdog organization from his boss, OMB Director Russell Vought, who has publicly commented that GAO should not exist. Ueland said Vought didn’t say much.
Hassan seemed skeptical.
“You’ve been nominated to serve as a watchdog over … an agency that your boss thinks shouldn’t even exist, and now you are claiming to this committee that you only had a single passing conversation with your current boss about your nomination to lead that agency,” she said. “Is that correct?”
Ueland said the most acknowledgment Vought gave was a head nod.
Other nominees
Senators also took up the nominations of:
- Michael Chamberlain to be director for the Office of Government Ethics
- Robert Steffens to be a governor for the United States Postal Service
- Jeffrey Zisk to be a commissioner for the Postal Regulatory Commission
- Maria D’Avanzo to be inspector general for the General Services Administration

- Robert Steinau to be inspector general for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration

The nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency declined to say whether he thinks CISA needs more staffing and resources, even as the cyber agency hires hundreds more people after widespread departures last year.
Meanwhile, Michael LoSapio’s nomination to be CISA director may also be in doubt after he said the Jan. 6, 2021, storming of the U.S. Capitol wasn’t an “attack.”
LoSapio, who is currently Palantir’s chief information security officer, appeared before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday alongside six other nominees.
LoSapio had kept a relatively low public profile prior to his nomination to be CISA director. Multiple senators focused their lines of questioning on him and his plans for CISA amid the packed nomination hearing.
Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.) referenced recent technology outages and asked how LoSapio would respond to similar scenarios as CISA director.
“It’s really important to understand the landscape of the systems that you have out in the wild, the things that you operate day to day, the systems that you rely on, the systems that are ancillary to the work you do, and do an extensive evaluation on their vulnerabilities, whether or not they’ve been patched or not, and how they have been architected and their defensive capabilities, both things we need to add and the things that exist today, as to how that maps to the threats we’re facing,” LoSapio responded.
Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) asked for LoSapio’s views on the Trump administration’s proposed $385 million cut to CISA’s budget for fiscal 2027, as well as the reduction of approximately 1,000 employees at the cyber agency since January 2025.
“I can’t comment on the current state of CISA because I’m not inside today,” he responded. “I’m coming from the private sector, and I can speak to my private sector experience about budgets and cuts and funding.”
Slotkin argued the recent outages and concerns about AI security point to the need for more CISA resources following the Trump administration’s cuts.
“I don’t necessarily believe more money means more security,” LoSapio responded. “I believe spending money on the right solutions in the right ways actually decreases risk.”
Meanwhile, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) asked all the nominees whether Jan. 6 was “an attack.”
LoSapio initially responded, “I don’t know,” before saying, “No, I don’t believe it was an attack,” and, “I wasn’t involved in politics. I know what I saw on the news.”
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who is retiring in January, told reporters he plans to put a hold on LoSapio’s nomination after those comments. His opposition narrows LoSapio’s path to confirmation, as he’s unlikely to be included in any Senate nominations package before Democrats take the majority in the upper chamber in the new year.
CISA has been without a Senate-confirmed director since January 2025. The Trump administration’s previous nominee to lead the agency, Sean Plankey, withdrew his name from consideration this spring after his nomination sat in the Senate for 13 months.
LoSapio’s nomination hearing comes a day after Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was also pressed on CISA staffing during a hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee.
Earlier this year, Mullin said CISA needs to hire 600 new staff following the loss of 1,000 employees between January 2025 and January 2026. And in September, acting CISA Director Nick Andersen said CISA was making progress on hiring, with roughly 250 new hires waiting to get through the security clearance process.
Asked by Homeland Security Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino (R-N.Y.) about the status of CISA hiring, Mullin said he “would follow up about the numbers.” But he said the Trump administration wants to increase CISA staffing, while alluding to the clearance process and government pay scales as hiring barriers.
“We’re able to meet those needs today, but we want to grow our capacity and to be able to do that, it does take time,” Mullin said. “But it also takes a long time to get people cleared to have a TS/SCI [clearance] and above level. Not everybody can pass those background checks … And we have to work with industry because our pay scale is much lower than what the industry is paying.”
Members of the Homeland Security Committee have also introduced a bipartisan bill that would establish a pilot program at CISA to help recruit AI and emerging technology experts.
“I think this is a very forward-leaning bipartisan bill that we need more of,” Mullin said. “This gives us exactly the flexibility we need to compete with industry, and bring in the best that we can into CISA, and pay them competitively.”
CISA has some existing authorities to pay cyber experts more competitively, including under the Department of Homeland Security’s Cybersecurity Talent Management System, or CTMS. However, CISA also scaled back some cyber pay incentives earlier this year, leading to concerns that more employees could leave the agency.
Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas), who was the lead House sponsor on the legislation creating CISA in 2018, pushed Mullin to prioritize recruiting at the agency.
“You have 600 people you need to hire,” McCaul said. “I would urge you to get CISA full steam, because the threats haven’t gone away and CISA needs to be in full force.”

sources.news_title: US Senate panel grills Trump cyber director about outages making people ‘jittery’ - Now Georgia
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (States Newsroom) — Members of the U.S. Senate Homeland Security Committee Thursday questioned the potential new head of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency about nationwide security disruptions that members of Congress said have left the American public on edge.
Democrats also accused the Trump administration of trying to quickly confirm that nominee and others during the lame-duck session of Congress, before Democrats gain majority control of the Senate in January. Democrats are set to come in with 56 seats.
Oklahoma Republican James Lankford, who is running to serve as the top GOP senator on the committee in the next Congress, defended President Donald Trump’s decision to make the nominations now.
“The White House seemed to have followed the letter of the law,” Lankford said. “I’m not completely sure they followed the entire spirit of the law, but they have actually gone through the process that needs to be done to be able to put the nominees forward, to be able to have the input.”
Trump nominated Michael LoSapio to be Director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, housed within the Department of Homeland Security. The agency handles election security and oversees protection of federal infrastructure from cyber attacks.
Senators also questioned at length a nominee who has generated opposition among Democrats, Eric M. Ueland, whom Trump has tapped to be comptroller general of the U.S. Government Accountability Office, the top federal government watchdog agency.
Scary tech outages
Widespread technology outages have occurred for days across the United States, including tens of thousands of canceled flights, transaction problems at major banks and shut-down email services at the National Security Agency.
Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a former national security federal government worker, grilled LoSapio about nationwide cyber outages.
“American citizens are jittery,” she said.
She raised concerns about the Trump administration’s decision to eliminate more than 1,000 positions at CISA. She asked LoSapio if he agreed with that decision and if he thinks CISA needs more funding.
LoSapio said he couldn’t comment “on the current state of CISA,” because he was coming in from the private sector. LoSapio is Palantir Technology Inc.’s chief information security officer.
LoSapio added that once he evaluates the agency, if he feels CISA needs more funding, he would ask Congress.
“I’m going to get involved and understand where the gaps are, and I will come back to this committee with the gap analysis,” he said.
Slotkin said she was not satisfied with his answer.
“At the end of the day, every American knows that cyberattacks are going up, that the risks are going up,” she said. “You should be able to say clearly, ‘There’s increasing threat, therefore, we need increasing resources to deal with it.’”
Connecticut Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal asked LoSapio about who won the 2020 presidential election, because CISA deals with election security. Trump has falsely claimed that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him, and galvanized a mob of his supporters to stop the certification of the election by storming the U.S. Capitol.
“I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” LoSapio said.
Blumenthal said LoSapio should not be allowed to run CISA if he couldn’t answer that former President Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election.
“You are disqualified from the position that you’ve been nominated to fill,” he said.
He then asked LoSapio if the U.S. Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021.
“I don’t believe it was an attack,” LoSapio said.
Blumenthal asked LoSapio if he was “alive on the planet” during the Jan. 6 insurrection.
LoSapio said he was.
Impoundments
GAO as the federal watchdog investigates fraud or violations of federal law. Ueland would serve for 15 years if confirmed by the Senate.
He currently works at the Office of Management and Budget, which has come under scrutiny from GAO for violating the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, which occurs when federal funds approved by Congress are withheld without congressional consent.
The Supreme Court last year allowed the Trump administration to move forward with withholding billions in foreign aid funding through what is called a pocket rescission, which means the president makes the request to cancel funds very late in the fiscal year.
But the court stopped short of making a decision on the merits of the case and whether the president has the authority to unilaterally impound congressional appropriations.
Michigan Democratic Sen. Gary Peters pressed Ueland about how GAO has found several times that OMB violated the federal impoundment law. He asked Ueland if he agreed with GAO’s conclusion.
Ueland declined to reach a conclusion.
“I’ve not had a chance to review those reports, and I took an affirmative decision not to because it was critical that if I am confirmed and have the privilege of serving as comptroller general, that I not prejudge or come to this committee with formed conclusions about what it is that GAO has rendered as advice to Congress,” Ueland said. “Instead, a clear commitment to continue to follow the process that GAO as comptroller general, is what I give to all of you.”
The chair of the committee, Kentucky Republican Sen. Rand Paul, asked Ueland if he would ignore a request by the Trump administration to stop an investigation.
Ueland said he would.
“We will fully follow through on charges from Congress, and in the event of obstacles, figure out ways to proceed to try to elicit information,” he said.
New Hampshire Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan questioned Ueland about the reaction to him leading the watchdog organization from his boss, OMB Director Russell Vought, who has publicly commented that GAO should not exist. Ueland said Vought didn’t say much.
Hassan seemed skeptical.
“You’ve been nominated to serve as a watchdog over … an agency that your boss thinks shouldn’t even exist, and now you are claiming to this committee that you only had a single passing conversation with your current boss about your nomination to lead that agency,” she said. “Is that correct?”
Ueland said the most acknowledgment Vought gave was a head nod.
Other nominees
Senators also took up the nominations of:
- Michael Chamberlain to be director for the Office of Government Ethics
- Robert Steffens to be a governor for the United States Postal Service
- Jeffrey Zisk to be a commissioner for the Postal Regulatory Commission
- Maria D’Avanzo to be inspector general for the General Services Administration
- Mark Priebe to be inspector general for the U.S. Department of Education
- Dennis Kirk to be inspector general for the U.S. Department of the Interior
- Robert Steinau to be inspector general for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration
- Eric Glover, Fernando Campoamor-Sanchez, Roman Chaban, and Bernard Desrosiers to be associate judges for the Superior Court of the District of Columbia

sources.text:
President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency refused to give a clear answer on who won the 2020 election and whether the events of Jan. 6, 2021, constituted an attack on the U.S. Capitol when questioned by lawmakers Thursday.
During a confirmation hearing before the Senate Homeland Security Committee featuring several other nominees, Michael LoSapio, currently the chief information security officer at Palantir, sidestepped questions about his perspective on thorny issues between the Trump administration and CISA.
The cyber defense agency has historically supported nationwide efforts to secure U.S. elections and came under fire in 2021 for saying the elections were “the most secure in American history,” despite Trump’s unsubstantiated claims that the results were rigged.
Over the last year, the Trump administration has significantly scaled back CISA’s election security efforts and urged the agency to focus on core missions, such as protecting critical infrastructure and providing cybersecurity support to federal agencies.
“I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” LoSapio said when Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) asked for his thoughts on who won the 2020 election. “My only involvement in the 2020 election was voting for the president of the United States.”
Blumenthal accused LoSapio of “ducking the question … in a way that betrays your lack of independence and objectivity” and said he was “disqualified from the position you have been nominated to fill.”
In another exchange with the senator, LoSapio said he did not believe the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection was an attack on the U.S. Capitol.
“I wasn’t involved in politics” at the time, he replied.
LoSapio’s responses are likely to infuriate Democrats, though he still stands a chance at confirmation with the current Republican Senate majority. Senate Homeland Security Chair Rand Paul (R-Ky.) criticized the events of Jan. 6 but defended LoSapio’s responses.
“It was big, it was huge and it shouldn’t be excused, it should be criticized,” Paul said during the hearing. “It was some attack, some riot, but it was also some people, and some of these people got locked up … that weren’t violent.”
A spokesperson for committee ranking member Gary Peters (D-Mich.) did not immediately respond to a request for comment on LoSapio’s responses.
The committee must vote on LoSapio’s nomination before the full Senate can. Paul told reporters after the hearing that he anticipates the committee will vote on LoSapio “in early December.”
CISA has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since January 2025, when former Director Jen Easterly stepped down. Trump previously nominated former Energy Department and Coast Guard official Sean Plankey for the role, but Plankey withdrew his nomination in April after it failed to advance in the Senate.
LoSapio would be coming into the role as the agency is rebounding from a series of layoffs and budget cuts that led to the agency losing about one-third of its staff last year.
When asked how he would approach agency staffing, LoSapio said he would “get involved and understand where the gaps are, and I will come back to this committee with the gap analysis.”
Gregory Svirnovskiy contributed to this report.
